content_metadata.description: This video tutorial demonstrates the chemical reaction between iron wool and chlorine gas to synthesize iron(III) chloride. It emphasizes safety precautions and the scientific process, highlighting both the challenges and successes of the experiment.

qAndA.answer: The chlorine gas appears yellowish in the jar.
qAndA.question: What color is the chlorine gas produced in the experiment?

qAndA.answer: Heating the iron wool increases its reactivity, making it more likely to react with the chlorine gas.
qAndA.question: Why does the host heat the iron wool before inserting it into the chlorine gas jar?

qAndA.answer: The iron(III) chloride solution is a brown color.
qAndA.question: What color is the iron(III) chloride solution at the end of the experiment?

qAndA.answer: The host explains that there was a limited amount of chlorine gas produced, which restricted the extent of the reaction.
qAndA.question: Why wasn't all of the iron wool consumed in the reaction?

qAndA.answer: The video starts with curiosity and excitement about the experiment, transitions to anxiety and tension during the more dangerous parts, and ends with a sense of satisfaction and accomplishment upon the successful creation of the iron(III) chloride solution.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, this is one better idea here today and today we're making iron III chloride.
That is iron.
Warning, this experiment involves toxic chlorine gas and fire.
I'm not responsible for any injuries from this experiment. Please proceed with extreme caution.
To start for this, we're going to need chlorine gas.
And for this, I evolved it from the electrolysis of brine solution using two carbon electrodes.
This took roughly about half an hour.
And you can see that it produced chlorine gas which I bottled in a jar and hydrogen gas which I just let float freely off.
And once I did that, I turned off the power and carefully took it out, putting the cap on the bottom,
and leaving a small amount of water in the bottom and turning upside down so note if it could escape.
Then what I did when I was ready, I flipped it over and carefully unscrewed the cap loosening it just so I could pull it off very quickly.
Now I took my iron wool which is my iron sample I'm doing and took off the cap and heated it up in a candle.
Now I stuck it into the jar and let it hang there.
As you can see, it didn't heat up very enough for this first one.
So I reheated it again and stuck it back in there.
This time it was able to take off but it never really fully evolved and I just got some iron oxide that evolved from when it was burning into the air.
So I took off the cap again, then pulled it out and heated it back up in some fire.
This time heating it up very much on all sides until it was glowing red, took off the cap and very quickly stuck it in there.
And almost immediately you can see the reddish brown gas coming off.
This is the iron 3 chloride.
Just let that burn in there and oxidize for a little while.
This iron 3 chloride is very soluble in the water so when I was done I just took the iron wool out carefully and shook it in the water.
It all dissolved in there to create this acidic brown solution at the bottom of the iron 3 chloride.
These are the results here. You can see it at the very bottom after I cleaned the salt off the side of the jar.
There's still quite a bit of iron wool left because there is very much chlorine that I used in this experiment.
So once again that was one bad idea and thank you.
